title: From Local Wells to Regional Water Governance: The Rise of Mekorot in Mandatory Palestine, 1930–1948
content: This article reconstructs the emergence of Mekorot, founded in 1937, as a transition from settlement-by-settlement water development to regional water governance in Mandatory Palestine. Drawing on Mekorot protocols, Kishon planning documents, Palestine Economic Corporation records, hydrogeological surveys, and contemporary water-law debates, it asks why a regional utility became attractive in the mid-1930s. The article argues that Mekorot arose from four interacting management problems: hydrological heterogeneity, fragmented capital investment, uncertain demand, and institutional fragmentation. Picard’s 1935–1936 survey showed that much of the western Jezreel Valley had weak or uneconomic local groundwater while fissure zones near the Carmel offered substantially larger yields. The Kishon project responded by pooling sources, capital, and consumers within a common system. By 1938 it reportedly included 18 wells, about 17 km of steel mains, several pumping stations, and contracts with 13 agricultural settlements covering approximately 4550 dunams of initial irrigation demand. Expansion toward Haifa diversified demand and allowed hydraulic costs, economies of network scale, and developmental tariff policy to be managed together. The case shows how regional water governance could emerge before sovereign state institutions while remaining politically bounded and environmentally consequential.
